The universe is constantly expanding (and the rate is increasing) at each and every point in spacetime. Imagine a deflated balloon with dots drawn all over it's surface at equal distances from one another. As you inflate the balloon, each and every point will expand away from one another at the same time (the fact the balloon expands into space around it is where the analogy breaks down, though). If you'd indulge me a little more -- this has some really interesting implications. Going back to the balloon analogy, if you would imagine 3 points in a line on the balloon, say points a, b, and c such that point b is between points a and c. As you can imagine, the speed at which the points a-b and b-c are expanding away from each other are the same. However, the points a and c are expanding away from each other twice as fast as they are expanding away from b. The implication if you didn't realise is that there are actually parts of the universe that are expanding away from each other faster than the speed of light. Pretty cool, huh?

Yeah, see this is an odd one. Because part of understanding the answer to that question, will be realizing that that question actually makes no sense.

There is no "outside the universe". All of space and time is within the universe, "outside" is literally non-existent. It's not a vacuum, not empty space; it's the complete absence of space-time. It's a logical construct only, and then really only necessary because our minds are used to things having an inside and an outside, and everything in the universe has both, but the universe itself does not.

This question is very similar to asking "what happened before the big bang?" There was no time before the big bang, so "before" is nonsensical in this context. Assume you have an infinite sheet of gridded paper. Pick any two points on that sheet and measure their distance. This is what we do when we measure the distance to another galaxy.

Now what we've measured is that all of these points are moving away from us, and the further they are, the faster they're moving. To stick with the paper analogy, imagine the paper is gradually growing larger and larger. It's infinitely large already, so it's not expanding into anything. But the distance between each and every grid point is continuously increasing. That's what it means for space to be expanding.

It's not a gas cloud filling up a void. It's the structure of space itself, wherein any and every two points will drift further and further from each other throughout time.

These colonial Grand Juries expressed their independence by refusing to indict leaders of the Stamp Act (1765), and refusing to bring libel charges against the editors of the Boston Gazette (1765). A union with other colonies to oppose British taxes was supported by the Philadelphia Grand Jury in 1770.
